extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, screenplay students, and writers learning three-act/beat-structure (especially beginners)
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Blake Snyder’s 15-beat 'Save the Cat' beat sheet to analyze or outline a three-act feature screenplay, with approximate page-number targets and illustrative examples (here using Legally Blonde).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening Image
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) The audience is first engaged with something compelling that sets the tone – and we begin to see how things as they are right now (they will be clearly different at the end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target page: 1. Shows the status quo and tone. Example: WE MEET SORORITY GIRL ELLE, AND SEE THAT SHE’S A GOOD PERSON BUT KIND OF SILLY, NAÏVE, WITH A LIMITED VISION OF WHAT HER LIFE COULD BE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme Stated
rubrics_metrics.description: (5) Usually spoken to the main character in a snippet of dialogue, this gives a sense of the deeper issues that this story is 'about.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target page: ~5. Often a line from another character that hints at the central thematic question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-Up Section
rubrics_metrics.description: (1–10) We meet the main character, who is living a compromised life in some way, while dealing with problems – and has something about them we can respect or like. We get a broad enough sense of their 'status quo' life to feel we understand them, and can begin to care about them. We see the world through their eyes, and will for the rest of the movie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target pages: 1–10. Presents the 'thesis' of their current life; no big crises yet but examples of life as it is. Example: early scenes establishing Elle’s personality and limited vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalyst
rubrics_metrics.description: (12) An event rocks the main character’s world completely, and sets in motion the central problem of the story. It’s an external problem (not just internal) that demands to be dealt with now – it has clear and present stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target page: ~12. Must be an externally felt event that forces the story to start. Example: WARNER BREAKS UP WITH ELLE. Note: the author warns the Catalyst should not be placed too early (audience needs attachment) or too late; keep around p.12 when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate Section
rubrics_metrics.description: (12–25) The main character questions what has happened, tries to figure out what to do, and often seeks to avoid the true 'call to adventure.' They take initial logical actions to try to fix things, which fail, narrowing their options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target pages: ~12–25. Shows attempts, doubts, and failed solutions leading to a decision to act. Example: ELLE REELS FROM THE BREAKUP, DECIDES TO TRY TO GET INTO HARVARD LAW and begins the necessary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break into Two
rubrics_metrics.description: (25) The main character enters an 'upside down world' – a new arena where they’re out of their element and overmatched as they attempt to confront the story problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target page: ~25. Marks the end of Act I/Start of Act II — the protagonist commits to the new world. Example: ELLE ARRIVES AT HARVARD LAW, HAVING BEEN ACCEPTED.

rubrics_metrics.name: B Story
rubrics_metrics.description: (30) A second story begins, which will run parallel to the 'A Story' and interweave with it; the theme and the character’s inner journey tends to be explored here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target page: ~30. Often the love story or a relationship arc, but it must present its own problem (it can't just be a relationship that’s going well). Example: ELLE MEETS PAULETTE, WHO HAS HER OWN PROBLEM WITH MEN.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fun and Games Section
rubrics_metrics.description: (30–55) The entertaining aspects of the story’s premise are explored (scenes that might appear in the trailer) — highlighting how the protagonist is unlikelier for this 'upside down world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target pages: ~30–55. These are the premise-driven set-pieces that are fun for the audience but 'hell' for the main character. Example: LIFE AT HARVARD IS HELLISH FOR ELLE; scenes showing her struggles and comic/entertaining moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: (55) The stakes are raised: the problem becomes more focused, more serious, more important and urgent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target page: ~55. A tonal/structural shift that escalates stakes; can be a false victory or setback. Example: ELLE GETS THE OPPORTUNITY TO WORK ON THE BIG CASE WITH BIG CONSEQUENCES.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad Guys Close In Section
rubrics_metrics.description: (55–75) There may be no specific 'bad guys,' but the problems should get worse and worse – the main character seems to be failing, facing more impossible obstacles, and relationships with allies tend to break down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target pages: ~55–75. Escalation, punch-counterpunch rhythms, increasing opposition. Example: WORK ON THE CASE IS DIFFICULT; setbacks accumulate; antagonistic forces gain ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: All Is Lost
rubrics_metrics.description: (75) The story seems to be over; the main character seems to have no hope — everything they were trying has failed and there are no other options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target page: ~75. This beat should feel like the story is over — the protagonist has hit the bottom. Example: ELLE IS OFF THE CASE, AND IS GOING TO LEAVE IN DISGRACE. The author emphasizes: 'All is lost' must feel hopeless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark Night of the Soul
rubrics_metrics.description: (somewhere between 75 and 85) The main character reels from the 'all is lost' moment — often a 'whiff of death' — and reflects on failure and identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target pages: ~75–85. Internal emotional low point where the protagonist questions who they are. Example: ELLE IS HUMILIATED AND QUESTIONING WHO SHE IS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break into Three
rubrics_metrics.description: (85) A new idea, new hope, or new plan for solving the story problem emerges — often the A Story and B Story cross and the B Story should be unresolved and at its worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target page: ~85. The protagonist finds a way forward (often informed by what was learned in the B Story). Example: ELLE GETS BACK ON THE CASE THANKS TO SUPPORT FROM FRIENDS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale Section
rubrics_metrics.description: (85–110) A five-part challenge akin to 'storming the castle': the hero fails at first, is pressed to their absolute limit, forced to confront their demons and possibly change, before the story problem is finally resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target pages: ~85–110. The climax sequence where tactics and character growth resolve the main problem. Example: ELLE WORKS TO WIN THE CASE; through this she discovers a new version of herself and resolves her goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Image
rubrics_metrics.description: (110) Reflecting the new status quo now that this story is over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target page: ~110. A visual or scene that contrasts with the Opening Image to show how things have changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page-count timing and rigidity guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate page-number targets are given for each beat (e.g., Catalyst ~12, Break into Two ~25, Midpoint ~55, All Is Lost ~75, Break into Three ~85, Final Image ~110).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly notes page counts are approximate and can be pro-rated for shorter scripts (e.g., 90–100 page scripts). Be cautious especially with Catalyst timing — if it comes before page 10 the audience may not be attached; the author recommends not skimping on Set-up. Don’t be overly rigid — small shifts of several pages are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Save the Cat as a tool, not a formula; preserve voice and authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: The beat sheet outlines common structural language of screen storytelling but reading/using it does not guarantee a good script; scripts that feel 'obvious' Save the Cat can be judged as formulaic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance from the author: the method is an accessible resource for writers (especially beginners) but great scripts need original voice, authenticity, and strong writing beyond just following beats. Avoid writing scripts that telegraph beats in an obvious/rote way (the 'bad SAVE THE CAT scripts' anti-pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ten story types / genres (Snyder)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to Blake Snyder’s ten story types or 'genres' as useful classification for core story ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes these ten story types fit well with focusing on a core idea, though the page does not enumerate them here. They are presented as a complementary tool for understanding how a story's central idea maps to structure.
